## Introduction

Why:

-   Flooding is a frequent and costly hazard in Northwest Florida\
-   Damage varies widely across flood events\
-   Understanding what drives this variability can help improve planning and mitigation efforts

Research Focus and Goal:

-   This study examines flood events across 16 counties in Northwest Florida\
-   Uses historical data on flood events, rainfall, and county characteristics\
-   The goal is to explore whether these factors can help explain flood damage

## Key Questions

::::: {.columns valign="center"}
::: {.column width="45%"}
### What drives flood damage?

-   Can rainfall patterns improve prediction?\
-   Do county-level characteristics matter?

### How can Machine Learning help?

-   Can Random Forest be used to predict flood damage?
-   If so, what variables are the most useful?
:::

```{r}
library(sf)
library(tigris)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

fl_counties <- counties(state = "FL", year = 2020)

nw_county_names <- c(
  "Escambia", "Santa Rosa", "Okaloosa", "Walton",
  "Holmes", "Washington", "Bay", "Jackson",
  "Calhoun", "Gulf", "Franklin", "Liberty",
  "Gadsden", "Leon", "Wakulla", "Jefferson"
)

nw_fl <- fl_counties %>%
  filter(NAME %in% nw_county_names) %>%
  mutate(NAME = factor(NAME, levels = nw_county_names)) %>%
  arrange(NAME) %>%
  mutate(id = row_number())

fl_counties_proj <- st_transform(fl_counties, 3086)
nw_fl_proj <- st_transform(nw_fl, 3086)

nw_labels <- st_point_on_surface(nw_fl_proj)
nw_labels$id <- nw_fl_proj$id

map_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = fl_counties_proj, fill = "gray90", color = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = nw_fl_proj, fill = "#4DA3FF", color = "black", size = 0.4) +
  geom_sf_text(data = nw_labels, aes(label = id), size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = st_bbox(nw_fl_proj)[c("xmin", "xmax")] + c(-50000, 30000),
    ylim = st_bbox(nw_fl_proj)[c("ymin", "ymax")] + c(-30000, 30000),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(title = "Northwest Florida Study Area") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16)
  )
```

## Statiscial Method: Random Forest

Random forest is a flexible, buildable, and straightforward machine learning method. Random forest produces hundreds of decision trees and binary splitting to determine the best split per possible variable. Each tree is trained with a random parameter, and the splitting function is used for the selection of the more fitting observable variable.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-random-forest
//| fig-cap: "Conceptual example of a random forest model showing multiple decision trees contributing to a final prediction."
//| fig-width: 8
//| out-width: 85%
//| fig-align: center
//| fig-show: hold

digraph random_forest_example {
  graph [layout=dot, rankdir=TB, nodesep=0.4, ranksep=0.6]
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=chartreuse3, fontname=Helvetica]
  edge [fontname=Helvetica]

  final [shape=ellipse, label="Final Prediction\n(Average of Trees)"]

  subgraph cluster_1 {
    label="Tree 1"
    t1a [label="Rainfall > 3 in?"]
    t1d [label="High Damage"]
    t1e [label="Low Damage"]
    t1a -> t1d [label="Yes"]
    t1a -> t1e [label="No"]
  }

  subgraph cluster_2 {
    label="Tree 2"
    t2a [label="Flash Flood?"]
    t2d [label="High Damage"]
    t2e [label="Moderate Damage"]
    t2a -> t2d [label="Yes"]
    t2a -> t2e [label="No"]
  }

  subgraph cluster_3 {
    label="Tree 3"
    t3a [label="Housing Units > 50k?"]
    t3d [label="Moderate Damage"]
    t3e [label="Low Damage"]
    t3a -> t3d [label="Yes"]
    t3a -> t3e [label="No"]
  }

  t1d -> final
  t1e -> final
  t2d -> final
  t2e -> final
  t3d -> final
  t3e -> final
}
```

Figure 1. Conceptual example of a random forest model showing multiple decision trees contributing to a final prediction.

## Features

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="33%"}
### Assumptions

-   Each tree makes its own decisions.\
-   Data points are chosen randomly to reduce mistakes.\
-   Sufficient data ensures the trees have unique patterns and variety.\
-   Combining the predictions from different trees leads to a more accurate final result.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
### Advantages

-   Easy to identify importance of features\
-   Multiple decision trees tend to cause little risk of overfitting (not too close to original training data)\
-   Very accurate due to multiple subgroups\
-   Less need for data management (pre-processing to perform random forest)
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
### Limitations

-   Slower to acquire observations for best decision making\
-   Bound by the lowest and highest observations (no extrapolate)\
-   Difficult to interpret the decisions of ‘best features’ seen with trees
:::
::::::

## Formula

Mean square error is used in random forest regression to determine the optimal splits during training and evaluate the model performance. The lower mean square error that is determined, the greater the model accuracy. The squared difference between actual and predicted values is squared (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². 1 over the number of observations averages the total squared error. The summation symbol Σ represents the summation of the observed data points (@hodson2021mean).

$$
MSE = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
$$

## Data Visualization

```{r}
#| label: fig-flood-event-pie
#| fig-cap: "Flash Flood vs Flood Events (2000–Present)"
#| fig-align: center

library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

stormevents <- read_csv("StormEvents_NWFL2.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(BEGIN_DATE_TIME = mdy(BEGIN_DATE)) %>%
  filter(BEGIN_DATE_TIME >= as.Date("2000-01-01"))

floodcountall <- stormevents %>%
  count(EVENT_TYPE) %>%
  mutate(percent = n / sum(n) * 100)

ggplot(floodcountall, aes(x = "", y = percent, fill = EVENT_TYPE)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(percent, 1), "%\n(", n, ")")),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
    color = "white",
    size = 6
  ) +
  labs(
    fill = "Event Type"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Flash Flood" = "blue2", "Flood" = "chartreuse3")) +
  theme_void()
```

## Flood Events Over Time

```{r}
#| label: fig-flood-damage-time
#| fig-cap: "Flood Events and Property Damage Over Time"
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7

library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

yearly_data <- stormevents %>%
  mutate(
    BEGIN_DATE = mdy(BEGIN_DATE),
    year = year(BEGIN_DATE),
    damage = as.numeric(DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(year)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    storms = n(),
    total_damage_millions = sum(damage, na.rm = TRUE) / 1000000,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

scale_factor <- max(yearly_data$storms, na.rm = TRUE) / 
  max(yearly_data$total_damage_millions, na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(yearly_data, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = storms, fill = "Flood Events"), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = total_damage_millions * scale_factor, color = "Total Damage"),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(y = total_damage_millions * scale_factor, color = "Damage Trendline"),
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(y = storms, color = "Frequency Trendline"),
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Legend",
    values = c("Flood Events" = "blue3")
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Legend",
    values = c(
      "Total Damage" = "chartreuse3",
      "Damage Trendline" = "red",
      "Frequency Trendline" = "orange"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Number of Flood Events",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(
      ~ . / scale_factor,
      name = "Total Property Damage (Millions of $)"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(min(yearly_data$year), max(yearly_data$year), by = 5)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Year") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

## Rainfall

```{r}
#| label: fig-monthly-rainfall-county
#| fig-cap: "Average Monthly Rainfall by County"
#| fig-align: center

library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

prec <- read_xlsx("Precp.xlsx")

monthly_avg <- prec %>%
  mutate(
    DATE = as.Date(DATE),
    rain_in = PRCP,
    year = year(DATE),
    month_num = month(DATE),
    month = month(DATE, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(DATE), !is.na(rain_in)) %>%
  filter(year >= 2020, year <= 2025) %>%
  group_by(County, DATE, year, month_num, month) %>%
  summarise(daily_rain = mean(rain_in, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(County, year, month_num, month) %>%
  summarise(month_total = sum(daily_rain, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(County, month_num, month) %>%
  summarise(avg_monthly_rain_in = mean(month_total, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(County, month_num)

ggplot(monthly_avg, aes(x = month, y = avg_monthly_rain_in)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue3") +
  facet_wrap(~ County, ncol = 4) +
  labs(
    x = "Month",
    y = "Average Rainfall (inches)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

## Model Explanation

-   Data was split using a 70/30 split.
-   Model 1 used 1-day, 3-day, and 7-day prior rainfall, population, housing units, and median home value to predict total damage.
-   Later models tested whether removing zero-damage events improved performance.
-   Model 4 simplified the predictor set to 1-day prior rainfall, population, housing units, and median home value.
-   The goal was to see whether a simpler model could better predict total flood damage.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(randomForest)
library(caret)
library(readxl)
library(zoo)

#-------------------------------
# 1. Flood events
#-------------------------------
flood_events <- stormevents %>%
  mutate(
    County = str_trim(CZ_NAME_STR),
    county_key = County %>%
      str_to_lower() %>%
      str_remove("\\s+county$") %>%
      str_trim(),
    BEGIN_DATE = mdy(BEGIN_DATE),
    EVENT_TYPE = str_trim(EVENT_TYPE)
  ) %>%
  filter(EVENT_TYPE %in% c("Flood", "Flash Flood")) %>%
  filter(BEGIN_DATE >= as.Date("2020-01-01")) %>%
  select(
    EVENT_ID,
    County,
    county_key,
    BEGIN_DATE,
    EVENT_TYPE,
    DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM,
    DAMAGE_CROPS_NUM,
    DEATHS_DIRECT,
    DEATHS_INDIRECT,
    INJURIES_DIRECT,
    INJURIES_INDIRECT,
    everything()
  )

nrow(flood_events)
table(flood_events$EVENT_TYPE)
names(flood_events)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false
#-------------------------------
# 2. County daily rainfall
#    Use MAX across gauges, not MEAN
#-------------------------------
county_daily_rain <- prec %>%
  mutate(
    County = str_trim(County),
    county_key = County %>%
      str_to_lower() %>%
      str_remove("\\s+county$") %>%
      str_trim(),
    DATE = as.Date(DATE)
  ) %>%
  group_by(County, county_key, DATE) %>%
  summarise(
    PRCP = max(PRCP, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# this should return 0 rows
county_daily_rain %>%
  count(county_key, DATE) %>%
  filter(n > 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false


#-------------------------------
# 3. Fill missing dates with 0 rain
#    so rolling windows are true 1-, 3-, and 7-day periods
#-------------------------------
county_daily_rain_complete <- county_daily_rain %>%
  group_by(County, county_key) %>%
  complete(
    DATE = seq(min(DATE, na.rm = TRUE), max(DATE, na.rm = TRUE), by = "day"),
    fill = list(PRCP = 0)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false

#-------------------------------
# 4. Prior-day rainfall windows
#-------------------------------
county_rain_windows <- county_daily_rain_complete %>%
  arrange(county_key, DATE) %>%
  group_by(county_key) %>%
  mutate(
    rain_1day_prior = lag(PRCP, 1),
    rain_3day_prior = lag(
      rollapply(PRCP, width = 3, FUN = sum, align = "right", fill = NA, partial = FALSE),
      1
    ),
    rain_7day_prior = lag(
      rollapply(PRCP, width = 7, FUN = sum, align = "right", fill = NA, partial = FALSE),
      1
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    rain_1day_prior = replace_na(rain_1day_prior, 0),
    rain_3day_prior = replace_na(rain_3day_prior, 0),
    rain_7day_prior = replace_na(rain_7day_prior, 0)
  )
county_rain_windows %>%
  select(County, county_key, DATE, PRCP, rain_1day_prior, rain_3day_prior, rain_7day_prior) %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(PRCP, rain_1day_prior, rain_3day_prior, rain_7day_prior), ~ round(.x, 3))
  ) %>%
  print(n = 20)



```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false


county_rain_windows <- county_daily_rain_complete %>%
  arrange(county_key, DATE) %>%
  group_by(county_key) %>%
  mutate(
    rain_1day_prior = lag(PRCP, 1),
    rain_3day_prior = lag(
      rollapply(PRCP, width = 3, FUN = sum, align = "right", fill = NA, partial = FALSE),
      1
    ),
    rain_7day_prior = lag(
      rollapply(PRCP, width = 7, FUN = sum, align = "right", fill = NA, partial = FALSE),
      1
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    rain_1day_prior = replace_na(rain_1day_prior, 0),
    rain_3day_prior = replace_na(rain_3day_prior, 0),
    rain_7day_prior = replace_na(rain_7day_prior, 0)
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false
flood_with_rain <- flood_events %>%
  left_join(
    county_rain_windows %>%
      select(county_key, DATE, rain_1day_prior, rain_3day_prior, rain_7day_prior),
    by = c("county_key", "BEGIN_DATE" = "DATE")
  )
flood_with_context <- flood_with_rain %>%
  left_join(
    census_data %>%
      mutate(
        County = str_trim(County),
        county_key = County %>%
          str_to_lower() %>%
          str_remove("\\s+county$") %>%
          str_trim()
      ) %>%
      select(county_key, Population, HousingUnits, MedianHomeValue),
    by = "county_key"
  )

names(flood_with_context)

flood_with_context %>%
  select(County, Population, HousingUnits, MedianHomeValue) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  print(n = 20)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false


flood_model_data <- flood_with_context %>%
  select(
    EVENT_ID,
    County,
    BEGIN_DATE,
    DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM,
    rain_1day_prior,
    rain_3day_prior,
    rain_7day_prior,
    Population,
    HousingUnits,
    MedianHomeValue
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    log_damage = log1p(DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM)
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false
flood_model_data %>%
  summarise(
    damage_missing = sum(is.na(DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM)),
    rain1_missing = sum(is.na(rain_1day_prior)),
    rain3_missing = sum(is.na(rain_3day_prior)),
    rain7_missing = sum(is.na(rain_7day_prior)),
    pop_missing = sum(is.na(Population)),
    housing_missing = sum(is.na(HousingUnits)),
    value_missing = sum(is.na(MedianHomeValue))
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false
flood_model_clean <- flood_model_data %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(log_damage),
    !is.na(rain_1day_prior),
    !is.na(rain_3day_prior),
    !is.na(rain_7day_prior),
    !is.na(Population),
    !is.na(HousingUnits),
    !is.na(MedianHomeValue)
  )

nrow(flood_model_clean)

summary(flood_model_clean)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false


set.seed(123)

train_index <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(flood_model_clean)),
  size = 0.7 * nrow(flood_model_clean)
)
```

## Model Performance Comparison

```{r}
#| label: fig-rsme-progression
#| fig-cap: "Random Forest Model Performance Comparison"
#| fig-align: center

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

model_results <- tibble(
  Model = c("Model 1\nAll Data",
            "Model 2\nDamage > 0",
            "Model 3\n+ Interactions",
            "Model 4\nFinal Reduced"),
  R2 = c(0.001039165, 0.04748602, 0.01711877, 0.05069955),
  RMSE = c(2.748546, 1.922366, 2.059047, 1.912249)
)

p1 <- ggplot(model_results, aes(x = Model, y = R2)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue3") +
 
  labs(
    title = expression(R^2 ~ "by Model"),
    x = NULL,
    y = expression(R^2)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p2 <- ggplot(model_results, aes(x = Model, y = RMSE)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue3") +
 
  labs(
    title = "RMSE by Model",
    x = NULL,
    y = "RMSE"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

(p1 + p2) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: false


results_m1 <- data.frame(
  actual = test_data$log_damage,
  predicted = pred,
  model = "Model 1"
)
results_m4 <- data.frame(
  actual = test_data2$log_damage,
  predicted = pred4,
  model = "Model 4"
)

results_all <- rbind(results_m1, results_m4)

results_all <- results_all %>%
  mutate(
    actual_dollars = exp(actual) - 1,
    predicted_dollars = exp(predicted) - 1
  )

```

## Predicted vs. Actual Flood Damage

```{r}
#| label: fig-predicted-vs-actual-log
#| fig-cap: "Predicted vs Actual Flood Damage for Model 1 and Model 4"
#| fig-align: center

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(results_all, aes(x = actual, y = predicted)) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(color = model), alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Model 1" = "chartreuse3",
    "Model 4" = "blue3"
  )) +
  labs(
    x = "Actual Log Damage",
    y = "Predicted Log Damage"
  ) +
theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
theme(
  legend.position = "none",
  strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
  panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray85"),
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
)
```

## Top Five Counties

```{r}
#| label: fig-top-five-counties
#| fig-cap: "Average Predicted Flood Damage by County"
#| fig-align: center

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Convert predictions from log back to dollars and create county summary
county_damage_rank <- test_data2 %>%
  mutate(predicted_damage = exp(pred4) - 1) %>%
  group_by(County) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_predicted_damage = mean(predicted_damage, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_events = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_predicted_damage))

# Keep top 10 counties
county_damage_rank_top <- county_damage_rank %>%
  slice(1:5)

# Plot
ggplot(county_damage_rank_top,
       aes(x = reorder(County, avg_predicted_damage),
           y = avg_predicted_damage)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_col(fill = "blue3")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = dollar) +
  labs(
    x = "County",
    y = "Average Predicted Damage ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Discussion

-   Random forest showed limited ability to predict flood damage (low R²)\

-   Flood damage likely influenced by missing variables\

-   Prior studies show elevation, slope, and proximity to rivers/streams are key factors

-   Limitations: limited variables; flooding influenced by geophysical factors

-   Future: additional variables needed to improve prediction

## Conclusion

-   Random forest showed **limited ability** to predict flood damage

-   Best model:

    -   1-day rainfall + population + housing + home value\
    -   excluded zero-damage events

-   Improvements:

    -   reduced noise\
    -   better actual vs predicted values

-   Highest damage counties:

    -   Washington, Walton, Liberty, Calhoun, Leon
